content: The use of glucocorticosteroids as an immunosuppressive therapy for myasthenia gravis is widely accepted, but their efficacy has rarely been evaluated in controlled studies. This review, which updates previous Cochrane reviews from 2005, 2006, and 2007, aimed to assess the effectiveness of glucocorticosteroids or adrenocorticotrophic hormone (ACTH) in treating autoimmune myasthenia gravis. To gather relevant data, a comprehensive search was conducted across multiple databases, including the Cochrane Neuromuscular Disease Group Specialized Register, the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials (CENTRAL), MEDLINE, and EMBASE, covering studies published up to June 2010. Additional data were sought by reviewing bibliographies of relevant studies and contacting authors to identify both published and unpublished information. The review included studies that were either quasi-randomized or fully randomized controlled trials. Participants included individuals of all ages and varying severities of myasthenia gravis. The interventions studied involved any form of glucocorticosteroid or ACTH treatment. Data extraction was performed by three authors and cross-checked by a fourth. Seven trials involving a total of 199 participants were included in the analysis. A trial investigating ACTH in 43 participants with ocular myasthenia gravis found no significant benefit compared to placebo. Two double-blind trials evaluated prednisone for generalized myasthenia gravis. In the first trial, which included 13 participants, the prednisone group showed slightly greater improvement at six months. In the second trial, involving 20 participants and conducted over a short-term period, the prednisone group demonstrated significantly greater improvement at two weeks. Two trials compared glucocorticosteroids with azathioprine, involving 41 and 10 participants, respectively. In one of these trials, the rate of treatment failure was higher in the prednisone group. Another trial compared glucocorticosteroids with intravenous immunoglobulin in 33 participants and found no significant differences in treatment responses over a 14-day period. An open-label trial with 39 participants assessed different corticosteroid doses and found that higher doses were associated with a shorter time to clinical improvement. However, none of these studies met the currently accepted standards for high-quality clinical trials. All included studies were at risk of bias and had limited statistical power. The authors concluded that limited evidence from randomized controlled trials suggests that corticosteroid treatment provides short-term benefits for myasthenia gravis when compared to placebo. This finding aligns with conclusions drawn from observational studies and expert opinions. However, there is insufficient evidence from randomized controlled trials to demonstrate a difference in efficacy between corticosteroids and either azathioprine or intravenous immunoglobulin.
